title: Why is the `main()` method declared `public` and `static`, and what is the purpose of the `String[] args` parameter?
shortTitle: Why main is public and static and the purpose of String[] args

s1_definition.profdef: The main method is the standard entry point the Java Virtual Machine invokes to start an application, and its exact signature public static void main of a String array is dictated by the launcher protocol. It is public so that the JVM, which lives outside the class's package, can access and call it. It is static so that the JVM can invoke it without first constructing an instance of the class, since at startup no objects exist yet and there is no obvious way for the JVM to know how to construct one. It returns void because there is no caller inside the program to receive a value, process exit status being communicated separately. The String array parameter carries the command-line arguments the user typed after the class or jar name, giving the program its external input at launch.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, main is like the single front door through which every customer enters the branch when it opens for the day. The door must be public because anyone from outside, meaning the JVM, has to be able to walk through it to start the day. It must be static because at opening time the branch is empty, there are no staff objects created yet, so the door must open on its own without needing a particular employee to let you in. The String array is like the slip of instructions the head office hands to the branch at opening, such as which mode to run in or which account file to process, so the branch knows what to do today. Without that exact door shape and the instruction slip, head office, meaning the JVM, cannot start the branch at all.
s1_definition.oneliner: main is public so the JVM can reach it, static so the JVM can call it without creating an object, returns void because no in-program caller receives a result, and the String array delivers the command-line arguments as the program's startup input.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The main method is the standard entry point the Java Virtual Machine invokes to start an application, and its exact signature public static void main of a String array is dictated by the launcher protocol. It is public so that the JVM, which lives outside the class's package, can access and call it. It is static so that the JVM can invoke it without first constructing an instance of the class, since at startup no objects exist yet and there is no obvious way for the JVM to know how to construct one. It returns void because there is no caller inside the program to receive a value, process exit status being communicated separately. The String array parameter carries the command-line arguments the user typed after the class or jar name, giving the program its external input at launch.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, main is like the single front door through which every customer enters the branch when it opens for the day. The door must be public because anyone from outside, meaning the JVM, has to be able to walk through it to start the day. It must be static because at opening time the branch is empty, there are no staff objects created yet, so the door must open on its own without needing a particular employee to let you in. The String array is like the slip of instructions the head office hands to the branch at opening, such as which mode to run in or which account file to process, so the branch knows what to do today. Without that exact door shape and the instruction slip, head office, meaning the JVM, cannot start the branch at all.

**One line to remember:** main is public so the JVM can reach it, static so the JVM can call it without creating an object, returns void because no in-program caller receives a result, and the String array delivers the command-line arguments as the program's startup input.

sections.s2_technical:
The JVM launcher looks for a method with the precise signature public static void main with a single String array parameter in the class named on the command line. Each part of that signature has a concrete reason. Public access is required because the launcher invokes the method reflectively from outside the class and its package, so any weaker access such as default or private would make the method unreachable and the JVM would reject it with an error that main is not accessible.

Static is required because the entry point must be callable before any instance of the class exists. When the program starts, the JVM has loaded the class but has created no objects, and it has no general way to decide which constructor to call or what arguments to pass. A static method belongs to the class itself and can be invoked with only the class loaded, so static removes the chicken-and-egg problem of needing an object to create the first object. If main were an instance method, the JVM would have to construct the class first, which it is not designed to do for the entry point.

Void is the return type because there is no caller within the Java program waiting for a value; the JVM launcher does not consume a return value from main. If the program needs to signal an exit code to the operating system, it calls System.exit with an int status rather than returning one, and a normal return from main simply ends the main thread.

The String array parameter carries the command-line arguments. When the user runs the program and types extra words after the class or jar name, the launcher packages those words, in order, as the elements of the array passed to main. So running the program with the words PROD and SAV2001 after the class name makes the array contain PROD at index zero and SAV2001 at index one. If no arguments are supplied, the array is empty with length zero, never null, so iterating it is always safe. The program reads these to configure itself, for example choosing an environment profile or an account id to process at launch.

Several senior points matter. First, the name args is only a convention; any legal identifier works, and the parameter can equivalently be written as varargs String with three dots, which the JVM accepts as the entry point because varargs compiles to the same array type. Second, the order of the modifiers can be static public but the usual convention is public static, and final may be added harmlessly. Third, main runs on a thread the JVM names main, and returning from it does not necessarily end the JVM if other non-daemon threads are still running. Fourth, in a real banking application built on a framework, developers rarely write raw argument parsing in main; instead main hands control to the framework, such as calling a Spring Boot run method that itself parses the arguments into configuration. Understanding the signature matters most for correctly launching batch jobs and command-line tools, where the arguments genuinely drive behavior such as which date's settlement to run.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The bank runs a nightly batch tool that must be started directly by the JVM with no objects pre-created, so it needs a valid entry point. This is exactly why main must be public and static with the precise signature.

Problem 2 — The operations team must tell the tool which environment to run in and which account to process at launch, without recompiling. This is exactly the purpose of the String array arguments.

Problem 3 — Sometimes the tool is run with no arguments and must behave sensibly rather than crash. This is exactly why the array is empty, not null, and why defaults are applied.

The code is a `BatchLauncher` main class that reads an environment profile and an account id from the command-line arguments, applies defaults when none are given, and processes a transfer for Rajesh, demonstrating every part of the signature.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
batch-launcher-demo/
├── src/
│   └── main/java/com/bank/batch/
│       └── BatchLauncher.java   (main — public static void main(String[]) + args usage)
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/batch/BatchLauncher.java

# Run with NO arguments → defaults apply (profile=dev, account=SAV2001)
java -cp out com.bank.batch.BatchLauncher

# Run WITH arguments → args[0]=prod, args[1]=CUR3001
java -cp out com.bank.batch.BatchLauncher prod CUR3001
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: either no command-line arguments, or the two words prod and CUR3001 supplied after the class name.

Step 1 — The user starts the program by naming the class on the command line. The JVM loads the BatchLauncher class but creates no objects. It then looks for the exact entry point, public static void main taking a String array, and because main is public it can reach it from outside, and because it is static it can call it with no instance.

Step 2 — The launcher gathers whatever words the user typed after the class name and packages them in order into the String array. If the user typed nothing extra, the array has length zero but is a real, non-null array.

Step 3 — Inside main, the program reads the profile from index zero and the account id from index one, falling back to dev and Rajesh's account when those indices are absent. This is how the external input configures the run without recompiling.

Step 4 — Being static, main runs immediately and only now constructs the first object, a BatchLauncher instance, demonstrating that the entry point itself needs no object but can create them once running.

Step 5 — The instance method runSettlement executes the real work, logging the chosen profile, amount, and account. When main returns normally, the main thread ends, and because no other non-daemon threads are running, the JVM exits with status zero.

Step 6 — The output differs between the two runs: with no arguments it reports zero arguments and the defaults, and with arguments it reports two arguments, profile prod, and account CUR3001, proving the String array delivered the command-line input.

```
# Run with no arguments
Oct 30, 2026 4:52:08 PM com.bank.batch.BatchLauncher main
INFO: Launched with 0 argument(s)
INFO: Profile   = dev
INFO: AccountId = SAV2001
INFO: [dev] Settling Rs.50000.00 for account SAV2001
INFO: Batch complete — main returning (exit status 0 by default).

# Run with: prod CUR3001
INFO: Launched with 2 argument(s)
INFO: Profile   = prod
INFO: AccountId = CUR3001
INFO: [prod] Settling Rs.50000.00 for account CUR3001
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  $ java com.bank.batch.BatchLauncher prod CUR3001
    │ OS passes words after class name
    ▼
  JVM launcher
    │ load class BatchLauncher (NO objects yet)
    │ find entry point: public static void main(String[])
    │   public → reachable from outside ✓
    │   static → callable with no instance ✓
    ▼
  main(args = ["prod", "CUR3001"])   ← length 0 (empty, not null) if none given
    │ profile   = args[0] else "dev"   → "prod"
    │ accountId = args[1] else "SAV2001" → "CUR3001"
    ▼
  new BatchLauncher()   ← FIRST object created, inside main
    │ launcher.runSettlement("prod","CUR3001")
    ▼
  settle Rs.50000 for CUR3001
    │ main returns (void) → main thread ends
    ▼
  no non-daemon threads left → JVM exits (status 0)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — main() Signature & args ═══

  ┌─ Key Rules ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  public  : JVM invokes from outside the package                    │
  │  static  : callable with class loaded, NO instance needed          │
  │  void    : launcher consumes no return; System.exit(code) for OS   │
  │  String[]: command-line args, in order; empty (len 0) not null     │
  │  'args' name is convention; String... varargs also valid           │
  │  main runs on the 'main' thread                                    │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: main only bootstraps + delegates; runSettlement does the work  │
  │  D: main wires objects, real logic lives in instance methods       │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │             BatchLauncher             │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  + static main(String[] args): void    │  ← JVM entry point
  │  ~ runSettlement(profile, id): void     │  ← instance work method
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── State: application startup ─────────────────────────────

  [CLASS LOADED, no objects]
       │ JVM invokes static main (public → reachable)
       ▼
  [main RUNNING on 'main' thread]
       │ parse args → create first object
       ▼
  [OBJECTS CREATED] → runSettlement → work done
       │ main returns (void)
       ▼
  [main thread ENDS] → no non-daemon threads → JVM EXITS (0)

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────

  1. JVM loads BatchLauncher
  2. invoke public static main(["prod","CUR3001"])
  3. profile="prod", accountId="CUR3001"
  4. new BatchLauncher() (first object)
  5. launcher.runSettlement("prod","CUR3001")
  6. settle Rs.50000 → log
  7. main returns → JVM exits 0
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The main method is the entry point the Java Virtual Machine calls to start an application, and the JVM requires its signature to be exactly public static void main taking a String array. Each modifier has a concrete reason. It is public because the JVM launcher invokes the method from outside the class and its package, so anything less accessible would make it unreachable and the JVM would refuse to start, reporting that main is not accessible.

It is static because the entry point must be callable before any object exists. At startup the JVM has loaded the class but created no instances, and it has no general way to know which constructor to call or what arguments to pass, so it cannot build an object just to invoke main. A static method belongs to the class itself and can be called with only the class loaded, which neatly solves the chicken-and-egg problem of needing an object to create the first object. If main were an instance method, the JVM would have to construct the class first, which the launcher protocol simply does not do.

It returns void because there is no caller inside the program waiting for a value; the launcher does not consume a return from main. When a program needs to tell the operating system its exit status, it calls System.exit with an integer code rather than returning one, and a normal return from main just ends the main thread. The String array parameter carries the command-line arguments: whatever words the user types after the class or jar name are packaged, in order, as the elements of that array, so the program receives its external startup input. If nothing is supplied the array is empty with length zero, never null, so iterating it is always safe.

In our banking system this matters most for batch tools and command-line jobs. A nightly settlement tool is launched directly by the JVM with no objects pre-created, which is exactly why main must be public and static, and the operations team passes the environment profile and the account or date to process as command-line arguments, which land in the String array, so they can change the run without recompiling. The senior details I add are that the name args is only a convention and any identifier works, that the parameter can equivalently be written as a String varargs because that compiles to the same array type, that main runs on a thread the JVM names main, and that returning from main does not kill the JVM if other non-daemon threads are still alive. In framework-based applications main usually just hands control to the framework, such as calling the Spring Boot run method, which then parses the same arguments into configuration. That precise understanding of the signature and the arguments is what lets me correctly build and launch the bank's batch jobs and tools.
